topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: CrewAI / AutoGen task decomposition
description: Two of the most widely adopted production multi-agent orchestration frameworks. In both, multi-intent handling is implicit: rather than an explicit splitter node, work is distributed across specialized agents defined by role/expertise. CrewAI (founded early 2024, Python, github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) declares agents with a role/goal/backstory and runs them via a Process: Sequential (tasks in fixed order), Hierarchical (an LLM manager agent decomposes the goal, delegates subtasks to worker agents based on their roles/tools, and aggregates), or Consensual (agents vote). AutoGen (Microsoft Research, late 2023, arXiv:2308.08155) models work as conversations between ConversableAgents (AssistantAgent, UserProxyAgent, GroupChatManager); decomposition emerges from multi-agent dialogue, with a GroupChatManager dynamically selecting the next speaker (RoundRobin/Selector/dynamic). Magentic-One (built on AutoGen) adds an explicit Orchestrator that maintains a task ledger and progress ledger. AutoGen has since evolved into the Microsoft Agent Framework. In both frameworks, routing = which specialized agent speaks/acts next, driven by a prompted manager/orchestrator LLM, not a dedicated decomposition+classification pipeline.
decomposition_method: LLM-prompted (zero-shot/CoT), implicit via role specialization. Neither uses a fine-tuned splitter, grammar, or embedding clustering. CrewAI hierarchical: the manager LLM (set via manager_llm or auto-created) reads the goal and breaks it into subtasks at runtime, dispatching to role-specialized worker agents; CrewAI sequential: the human pre-declares the task list (decomposition is authored, not generated). AutoGen: decomposition is emergent from a prompted multi-agent conversation — a planner/orchestrator agent (or the GroupChatManager) proposes subtasks and routes them to specialist agents through dialogue (Magentic-One formalizes this with an Orchestrator that writes a plan into a task ledger). Hybrid in practice: human-authored agent roles + LLM-generated subtask delegation.
decomposition_granularity: tool call to milestone+steps. Each routed unit is typically a coarse subtask assigned to one specialist agent (e.g. 'research X', 'write the report'), i.e. milestone-level work that the receiving agent further executes (often via its own internal ReAct-style tool loop). CrewAI's unit is a Task object bound to an agent; AutoGen's unit is a conversational turn/sub-goal handed to a specialist. So granularity is agent-assignment / milestone+steps rather than single tool calls.
ordering_strategy: Mixed. CrewAI Sequential = fixed sequential (each task output feeds the next). CrewAI Hierarchical = dynamic (the manager re-decides delegation based on real-time results), though tasks still follow a logical order. AutoGen = dynamic (mid-chain re-plan): the GroupChatManager/Orchestrator selects the next speaker turn-by-turn from conversation context, and Magentic-One's Orchestrator re-plans when the progress ledger stalls. Neither builds an explicit topological DAG of subtasks by default (no dependency-annotated graph planner); ordering is either author-fixed or conversation-dynamic. Limited true parallel fan-out (CrewAI added async/parallel task options; AutoGen is largely turn-based).
decomposition_validation: Largely none / blind trust in the manager LLM, with guardrail-style mitigations rather than a formal validator. Neither framework ships an AOP-style detector + reward model that checks solvability, completeness, and non-redundancy before dispatch. CrewAI relies on guardrails: clear task specs, bounded delegation (allow_delegation flags), max_iter caps, and task-level output validation/guardrail callbacks. AutoGen relies on termination conditions (max rounds, 'TERMINATE'/'DONE' tokens, satisfaction checks) and human-in-the-loop (UserProxyAgent) to catch bad decompositions; Magentic-One's progress ledger gives a lightweight self-check on whether the plan is advancing, triggering re-planning, but this is progress monitoring, not pre-dispatch decomposition verification. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: two-level (manager/orchestrator over worker agents), extensible to multi-level. CrewAI Hierarchical is explicitly manager -> worker (and crews can be nested as flows for deeper trees). AutoGen GroupChat is orchestrator/manager over participant agents, and nested chats / hierarchical GroupChats allow multi-level structures. Default usage is two-level; deeper nesting is possible but author-constructed.
router_type: graph/role-based manager planner per turn, i.e. an LLM manager that decides which agent handles each subtask. Not a single-/multi-label classifier and not an upfront full-DAG planner. CrewAI hierarchical: the manager agent picks the worker by matching subtask to agent role/tools (a prompted selection over the crew). AutoGen: speaker selection by the GroupChatManager (RoundRobinGroupChat = rule-based rotation; SelectorGroupChat / default GroupChatManager = LLM-prompted next-speaker choice from context). So router_type ranges from rule-based round-robin to LLM next-agent selection.
routing_model: prompted LLM (same family as the agents), hybrid with rule-based options. CrewAI manager routing is done by the manager_llm. AutoGen next-speaker selection is LLM-prompted (Selector/default manager) or rule-based (RoundRobin) or fully custom (user-supplied selection function). No fine-tuned classifier, embedding-similarity router, or RL-trained router by default; routing intelligence comes from the prompted manager/orchestrator plus author-defined role descriptions.
handles_ambiguity: best-effort pick, with human-in-the-loop as the main escape hatch. The manager/orchestrator commits to whichever specialist its prompt deems most appropriate; there is no abstain, no POMDP, no automatic uncertainty model. AutoGen's distinctive option is human-in-the-loop via UserProxyAgent (human_input_mode), letting a person resolve ambiguity or approve/redirect — the closest thing to a clarification mechanism, but it is developer-configured, not a learned when-to-ask policy. CrewAI mitigates ambiguity through clearer role/backstory boundaries and bounded delegation rather than asking the user. Net: overconfident best-effort routing with optional human override. [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: retry / re-delegate within the loop, or escalate to human. If no agent cleanly fits, CrewAI's manager re-delegates (subject to max_iter) and tasks can specify guardrails/fallback outputs; allow_delegation lets agents pass work to peers. AutoGen continues the conversation (manager picks another speaker) until a termination condition fires, or routes to the UserProxyAgent (human escalation). Persistent failure ends via termination (max rounds / 'TERMINATE') yielding a degraded final answer rather than a hard abort. No automatic route-to-general-LLM-with-re-decomposition primitive beyond the manager re-planning. [uncertain]
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: full-context over a small, hand-curated agent/tool set — neither framework is built for hundreds/thousands of skills via retrieval. Routing scales with the number of agents (typically a handful to dozens), all described in the manager's prompt; there is no built-in embedding retrieval, two-stage coarse-to-fine filter, or skill-tree traversal for routing among agents. Large crews inflate the manager prompt. (Tools per agent are similarly listed in-context.) CrewAI/AutoGen do support RAG/vector memory for knowledge, but that is content retrieval, not agent/skill routing retrieval. [uncertain]
router_agent_asymmetry: Low / none by default. The manager/orchestrator routes using each agent's role/goal/backstory (CrewAI) or system message/description (AutoGen) — roughly the same descriptive metadata the agent itself carries. There is no deliberate design where the router sees richer skill text than the executing agent (the SkillRouter asymmetry); both see role descriptions. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: Mixed: sequential chain (CrewAI Sequential), manager-delegated turn-based (CrewAI Hierarchical), and conversational round-based dispatch (AutoGen GroupChat). Fundamentally turn-based / dialogue-driven rather than DAG fan-out. CrewAI added asynchronous/parallel task execution options, but the dominant pattern is sequential or manager-coordinated turns; AutoGen is conversation-turn based (one speaker per round). Each specialist agent typically runs its own internal ReAct-style tool loop when executing its assigned subtask.
parallel_vs_concurrent: Mostly sequential/turn-based; limited concurrency. AutoGen GroupChat advances one speaker per round (not concurrent). CrewAI supports async tasks (async_execution) and kickoff_for_each / parallel flows for true concurrent execution of independent tasks, but this is opt-in, not the default. Neither emphasizes single-API-turn parallel tool calling the way LLM-Tool Compiler does; concurrency, where present, is at the task/agent level. [uncertain]
dependency_detection: explicit-by-authoring (CrewAI Sequential: task order + context= links declare dependencies) or LLM-implicit (Hierarchical/AutoGen: the manager/orchestrator infers ordering from conversation state). No learned dependency classifier and no automatic DAG inference; CrewAI lets the developer pass prior task outputs as context to express dependencies, otherwise dependence is whatever the manager LLM reasons. Default posture is assumed-sequential.
result_aggregation: LLM joiner / iterative. CrewAI Hierarchical: the manager agent synthesizes worker outputs into the final deliverable; Sequential: each task output is passed forward and the last task's output is the result (iterative chaining, optionally with a final synthesis task). AutoGen: the final answer is produced from the accumulated GroupChat conversation history (the shared message log acts as a sequential blackboard), often with a designated agent composing the result; Magentic-One's Orchestrator compiles the final answer from the ledger. So aggregation is an LLM re-reading shared state, not a typed structured merge.
mid_chain_feedback: hard (dynamic re-planning) for Hierarchical/AutoGen; soft for CrewAI Sequential. AutoGen's manager re-selects speakers based on intermediate messages and Magentic-One re-plans when the progress ledger detects no progress (explicit re-planning). CrewAI Hierarchical managers adjust delegation to real-time results. CrewAI Sequential is soft: later tasks receive earlier outputs as context but the task order is fixed (no re-planning node).
benchmark_name: No native benchmark; both are frameworks evaluated indirectly. AutoGen is evaluated via AutoGenBench on GAIA, AssistantBench, WebArena, HumanEval, math/coding tasks; Magentic-One (AutoGen-based) reports on GAIA, AssistantBench, WebArena. CrewAI is more often compared in framework-comparison studies (GAIA-style tasks, latency/cost/success-rate, e.g. vs LangGraph/AutoGen) rather than a canonical paper benchmark. Common external benchmarks: GAIA, AgentBench, WebArena, TAU-bench, SWE-bench.
multi_intent_coverage: Indirect / via benchmark choice. The frameworks themselves do not define multi-intent categories; coverage depends on the benchmark run on them. GAIA/AssistantBench/WebArena tasks are multi-step and often compound (mixed sequential + some independent sub-goals), so the frameworks are exercised on mixed multi-intent workloads, but there is no native parallel/multiple/parallel_multiple tagging (unlike BFCL v3). [uncertain]
accuracy_metric: Inherited from the benchmark used — typically outcome-based: GAIA uses exact-match against ground-truth final answers; WebArena uses end-to-end task success rate; AssistantBench success rate. Framework comparisons report task success rate plus latency and cost per task. No native AST-based or process-supervision metric in the frameworks themselves. [uncertain]
clarification_capability: Partial via human-in-the-loop, not measured as a metric. AutoGen's UserProxyAgent (human_input_mode = ALWAYS/TERMINATE/NEVER) can pause to ask a human, the closest built-in clarification hook; CrewAI agents can be configured to request human input on a task. But neither implements a learned when-to-ask vs. when-to-answer policy nor is evaluated on clarification efficiency (ClarifyBench/InteractComp/ClarEval). Clarification is a developer-enabled feature, not an evaluated capability. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: Outcome-only in headline evaluations (final-answer success rate). Magentic-One's task/progress ledgers provide some intermediate-progress signal operationally, but evaluation reports outcome metrics; no learned process-reward model scores intermediate decomposition steps. [uncertain]
eval_stability: Low / live-API and infrastructure-sensitive. Evaluations depend on live LLM APIs and live tool/web environments (GAIA, WebArena), so numbers drift with model/API changes; no cached/virtual API server like StableToolBench. AutoGenBench mitigates with fresh Docker containers per task and repeated runs for variance, but absolute numbers vary with hosting tier (reports of ~18 pts accuracy drop dev->tight serverless tier). [uncertain]
integration_pattern: standalone orchestration framework / library (application-layer). CrewAI: a Python library where you define Agents, Tasks, and a Crew with a Process; orchestration runs in-process. AutoGen: a Python (and now .NET) library of ConversableAgents + GroupChat, run in-process or via AutoGen Studio (UI); Magentic-One is a packaged multi-agent system on top. Both are application-layer; neither pushes routing into an inference-engine or proxy layer. Often embedded as the agent layer behind an app/service.
routing_layer: application-layer. Manager/orchestrator routing and speaker selection happen entirely in the application/library layer via LLM prompts; no inference-engine-layer or Envoy/ext_proc routing.
latency_overhead: Moderate-to-high; grows with agents and conversation turns. Every delegation/speaker-selection is an extra manager LLM call, and multi-agent dialogue multiplies round-trips (AutoGen open-ended reasoning is noted at ~5-6x the cost of leaner setups). There is no separate one-shot decomposition cost; instead overhead is amortized across many manager + agent turns. CrewAI is reported faster/cheaper than AutoGen for simple linear workflows; AutoGen costs more but handles open-ended reasoning. Each specialist's internal tool loop adds further calls. [uncertain]
online_adaptation: static at deploy. Routing/delegation behavior is fixed by prompts, role definitions, and manager logic; no bandit/RL or log-driven fine-tuning of the router. Both offer memory (short-term, long-term, entity/vector memory) that improves context over time, but that is content/episodic memory, not learned routing improvement from production feedback. [uncertain]
adoption: Production deployment + open-source, two of the most widely adopted multi-agent frameworks. CrewAI (open-source; reports serving a majority of Fortune 500 and hundreds of millions of agentic workflows/month, plus a commercial CrewAI Enterprise/AMP offering). AutoGen (open-source, Microsoft Research; AutoGen Studio UI; now evolving into the Microsoft Agent Framework SDK, with Magentic-One as a reference system). Both have large communities and commercial backing.
